catalog_quote: [Kimball 1994, Introduction 'Accents'] Pitch accent in nominal forms is lexical in nature. Every noun must have an accented syllable. The vast majority of root (i.e., underived) nouns have regular accentuation based on the shape of the penultimate syllable of the word; if the penultimate syllable has a long vowel, that syllable bears the accent; if the penultimate syllable does not have a long vowel, then the ultima bears the accent. ... [Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015: 106, 114] Koasati displays a complex prosodic system featuring intonation, lexical and grammatical tone, and predictable stress. ... These different melodies are phrase-final rather than lexical. ... [fn. 8] Kimball (1991:26–28) also describes a system of pitch accent, but it is quite different from what we hear. ... audit.recode_to: Resolve 'descriptions disagree' in favour of the Gordon/Martin analysis: word-level primary stress fixed on the FIRST syllable (location quantity-insensitive; cues F0 peak + intensity), heavy syllables (CVV, CVC) additionally prominent, no rhythmic/iambic footing; lexical and grammatical (grade) tone on the stem penult; Kimball's noun 'penult-if-long-else-ultima' accent = phrase-final AP/IP intonation per GML 2015 ICPhS sec. 3.1-3.3 and Gordon & Martin 2023: 282-283, 302. Keep Kimball 1991/1994 as the recorded dissent and keep the G&M hedge ('variable in its realization', 'plausibly due to word stress') in the caution field; weight_class CVV+CVC stands.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations are verbatim in held files (Kimball 1994 'Accents'; GML 2015 p.106 fn.8 and p.114 in lines 925-947, 1200-1236). Kimball 1991 pp. 26-28 not held. (2) Deciding sources are primary and good (2015 IJAL instrumental study vs. the grammar author's own 1994 restatement), but the 2015 stress analysis was self-described as tentative, which is why the record was left as an unresolved conflict. sources.quote: p.282: 'In Koasati, the first syllable is characteristically the most prominent one (Gordon et al. 2015a), where the prominence is associated most saliently with higher fundamental frequency and increased intensity. The prominence on the first syllable, however, is variable in its realization depending on context and speaker. The higher pitch on the first syllable may be superseded by a phrase-final rise or by a pitch peak on a word that precedes it within a close syntactic constituent'. p.283: 'the intensity is still greatest on the first syllable suggesting that it retains some prominence, p
sources.note: Latest statement by the instrumental team; drops the 2015 'tentative' framing for initial prominence, keeps CVV+CVC heavy, and explicitly files Kimball 1991's final prominence under phrase-level effects - bears directly on whether our 'conflict' coding should be resolved.

sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew, Jack Martin & Linda Langley. 2015. Prosodic structure and intonation in Koasati. In Proceedings of the 18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2015), Glasgow.
sources.quote: sec. 3.1: 'The smallest readily identifiable prosodic unit is the prosodic word, which is the domain of stress assignment. Primary stress in Koasati falls on the first syllable of a word and is associated with the highest F0 and greatest intensity in the word.' Abstract: 'predictable accents may dock on the penultimate syllable of the stem and on heavy syllables (those containing a long vowel or a coda sonorant)'. Accentual Phrase = initial and final H tone, typically isomorphic to the prosodic word; IP boundary tones L%/LH% statements, H% questions, HL% commands; lexical noun tone = LH rise '
sources.locator: Abstract; sec. 3.1 'Prosodic structure' (p.1); sec. 3.3 'Pitch accents' (pp.2-3); sec. 4
sources.note: States flatly 'Primary stress in Koasati falls on the first syllable of a word' and gives the AP/IP tonal grammar that explains Kimball's noun-final high as phrasal; also gives a different heavy criterion for accent docking (long V or sonorant coda).
